children: Midmarket firm NorthSands Capital is anchoring a $510 million investment to extend Peterson Partners' ownership of Kelso Industries-a bet that demand for parts and services to keep critical infrastructure running in data centers, healthcare facilities and manufacturing plants will remain a mainstay of the U.S. economy.

New York-based NorthSands, founded by Blackstone veteran dealmaker Bruce McEvoy, invested more than $450 million in the Kelso continuation vehicle, while Peterson in Salt Lake City reinvested through its latest flagship fund, according to the firms. The deal also marks an exit for Paceline Equity Partners, which first backed the company in 2023.

"In a world where there's uncertainty in a number of different sectors and industries, mechanical, electrical, plumbing is not going anywhere," said McEvoy, whose firm focuses on secondary market deals including such single-asset transactions. "If a hospital's air-conditioning unit breaks, it's going to get fixed or replaced."
Further, he said, the investment taps into two high-growth areas: the reshoring of U.S. manufacturing and the data-center boom.
Private equity has long sought to capitalize on companies, such as Kelso, that offer "mission critical" services that are needed across economic cycles.

Continuation vehicles, which buyout firms often use to retain their best performing assets while giving earlier fund backers a way to cash out, are among a broader group of secondary deals that reached record levels in this year's first half as fund sponsors sought to increase cash returns to their investors amid a slowdown in outright exit deals.

Investment bank Evercore tallied about $121 billion in secondary-market transactions this year through June, while Jefferies Financial Group estimated the value at around $118 billion. Both firms put the market on track to reach an annual record.

Continuation vehicles dominate general partner-led secondary transactions, with single-asset deals like the one for Kelso accounting for more than half of that activity, according to Evercore and Jefferies.
Kelso, established in 2021 with early backing from Peterson, focuses on providing services to commercial and industrial customers, including data center operators, healthcare providers and airports.
The kind of projects Kelso takes on are considered nondiscretionary work that must be done regardless of the ups and downs of the broader economy, Peterson partner Spencer Clawson said.

Based near Salt Lake City in Draper, Utah, the company has grown rapidly through acquisitions to more than 4,000 employees and over $1 billion in annual revenue, providing new installations as well as performing services including maintenance and repairs, he said.

Kelso was founded by childhood friends Steve Carroll and Steve Nicholson, who are chief executive and chairman of the company, respectively. While retaining those roles, Clawson said, the co-founders also will continue Kelso's acquisitive strategy "in line with what we've done in the past."

Kelso has acquired some 40 businesses through a roll-up strategy, according to Schryver & Co., which advises commercial and residential services companies on mergers and acquisitions. Owners of the businesses Kelso buys typically retain minority stakes and continue running the operations under their original brands.
